That is an important first step. The General Assembly should pass the bill now so the Commonwealth has time to fully evaluate the environmental and economic impacts on our communities.
New York has also begun to act. Governor Kathy Hochul ordered a 1-year moratorium on the largest data centers while the state examines their energy impacts. The legislature should build on that action by extending the moratorium to at least 3 years, and Governor Hochul should sign that stronger protection into law.

clean_body: A 3-year pause gives communities time to understand the real costs before corporations lock them in for decades. | | Peter, Big Tech is pouring billions of dollars into a massive expansion of data centers to fuel artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency mining, cloud computing, and other technologies. Communities are being asked to accept the consequences before the full costs are even understood. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water while increasing pressure on the electric grid, contributing to higher utility costs, producing around-the-clock noise, adding pollution -- all while Big Tech corporations demand public subsidies. By 2030, data centers are projected to consume 12% of all U.S. electricity, roughly triple their current share and equal to all other industries combined. Working families should not be forced to subsidize an industry dominated by some of the richest corporations on Earth while communities are left with higher bills and strained resources. No neighborhood should become a sacrifice zone for Big Tech's expansion. | | Pennsylvania lawmakers have already introduced Senate Bill 1359, which would establish a 3-year statewide moratorium on the development and permitting of new hyperscale data centers. That is an important first step. The General Assembly should pass the bill now so the Commonwealth has time to fully evaluate the environmental and economic impacts on our communities. New York has also begun to act. Governor Kathy Hochul ordered a 1-year moratorium on the largest data centers while the state examines their energy impacts. The legislature should build on that action by extending the moratorium to at least 3 years, and Governor Hochul should sign that stronger protection into law. Every state should give communities the same power to determine what happens next. Corporate developers should not be allowed to rush projects through before residents understand what they could mean for their water, electricity bills, health, environment, and local economy. Together, we’re demanding critical protections for our communities, not more handouts to big corporations. -OnePA | OnePA is a 501(c)4 organization Contributions to OnePA are not tax deductible for federal income tax purposes Our mailing address is P.O. | | **The ‘Unprecedented’ Sanctions Have a Concrete Blueprint: the July 14 Action Named 50+ Entities Across the UAE, Singapore, Hong Kong, and India. Here Is What the Campaign Targets — and the Coming Test of Whether It Reaches China.**
---
| | The ‘unprecedented’ sanctions campaign Bessent promised has a concrete template already on the books. On July 14, 2026, OFAC expanded sanctions targeting the alleged illicit shipping network of Iranian businessman Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, citing its role in facilitating Iran’s oil exports after renewed attacks near Hormuz. **The action sanctioned more than 50 individuals, companies, and vessels linked to the network across the UAE, Singapore, Hong Kong, India, and other jurisdictions — a multi-jurisdictional strike at the shadow architecture that moves Iranian crude.**
---
| | For your portfolio, the Shamkhani action is the blueprint for what ‘economic isolation’ means in practice. By naming entities across multiple countries, OFAC signaled the campaign targets not Iran directly — already heavily sanctioned — but the international network of intermediaries and shippers that enables Iranian oil to reach buyers. **This is the shadow-fleet system: the transponders-off tankers, front companies, and third-country facilitators that keep 9 million barrels a day flowing despite the blockade.** The coming measures are almost certainly an escalation of this approach — more names, more jurisdictions, and critically, whether they finally reach China, the destination for most sanctioned crude. For the American investor, this clarifies both mechanism and limit: a widening net raises the cost of the trade without stopping it, and as long as it targets intermediaries rather than Chinese end-buyers, it lifts the premium at the margin without cutting the flow that keeps oil range-bound. Watch the jurisdictions named next: more UAE and Singapore means more of the same; named Chinese refiners would signal genuine escalation.

| | Fellow Patriot, this is your Vice President.

_**It feels like I typed and re-typed this note close to 100 times before I knew just how I wanted to say this. **_

**Not because I questioned my message, but because of just how critical it is that this message be received clearly. **

**Truthfully, this is more personal and from the heart than most messages, because it's going to patriots that I feel I can trust as our movement’s closest confidants.**

Every time I stand behind the resolute desk, or walk into a critical cabinet meeting to make a decision surrounded by the most dedicated and fearless men and women in our country, I feel the very weight of our country’s survival in my hands and the responsibility of what it represents — a thin, fragile line between the America we love and the America the radical left is determined to build in its place.

_And when I sit alone with my thoughts and my prayers the question I ask myself constantly is**“what more can I do?” **_

**_[That’s when I decided I needed to write this message. ](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyc0D2u3CAUBeDV4A4L8A9M4SLSyFKKl-YVKa1ruPbcBIMF1zPJ7qMpsoG3gfOdc35-LB9AkdL-Aw6cqNal1IUe8ETY4JkLZ6i_IQU69kxpMcqMUjmp3QKe6YlLD02YBqPd5hqctHVWjWbQqnlM1nUWPHTbzYbb2q_B4U351Y8b3HAwQ0PTO0857XSvB2Vb5YbNarcB4Gg770SvrjMAY0upUsDqcz7PHInJ1zaXvYnTg_msovsmzCzMXNFfBdsXpYKh9fkQZl4LpJCT3ClGueUiGf9AFWb-FSBGDyXUnBjWiJLLxY_tivHvkQueWGpOECUe8oQ30M3lDRRKu-juXC4UZrz4WNiL7v7981P-XyTMCAefuRJTTqK766ZM4XxRjFRHK3q1H0DxXbHhLx7_nMy_AAAA__-JApbX)_**

At the end of my life, I want to stand before God Almighty and be able to say with a clear conscience that I gave everything I had to protect the soul of this country.
**[I _’m coming to you because I believe you're someone who understands what's happening to this country as clearly as I do. _](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyc0D2u3CAUBeDV4A4L8A9M4SLSyFKKl-YVKa1ruPbcBIMF1zPJ7qMpsoG3gfOdc35-LB9AkdL-Aw6cqNal1IUe8ETY4JkLZ6i_IQU69kxpMcqMUjmp3QKe6YlLD02YBqPd5hqctHVWjWbQqnlM1nUWPHTbzYbb2q_B4U351Y8b3HAwQ0PTO0857XSvB2Vb5YbNarcB4Gg770SvrjMAY0upUsDqcz7PHInJ1zaXvYnTg_msovsmzCzMXNFfBdsXpYKh9fkQZl4LpJCT3ClGueUiGf9AFWb-FSBGDyXUnBjWiJLLxY_tivHvkQueWGpOECUe8oQ30M3lDRRKu-juXC4UZrz4WNiL7v7981P-XyTMCAefuRJTTqK766ZM4XxRjFRHK3q1H0DxXbHhLx7_nMy_AAAA__-JApbX)__**

And when I sit alone with my thoughts and my prayers the question I ask myself constantly is“what more can I do?” At the end of my life, I want to stand before God Almighty and be able to say with a clear conscience that I gave everything I had to protect the soul of this country. | | | Good morning, team!

I’m writing you a quick message this morning before heading out to meet with voters during today’s primary election in Alaska.

**If you can afford it today, I’m humbly asking for you to make a contribution to my campaign and Equal Opportunity Now for Primary Day today.**

I’m sorry to be so upfront because – to be honest – Yup’ik people don’t like asking for money. In fact, I hate it! But I wouldn’t ask if your support wasn’t so important.

The reality is that today is the biggest moment for our campaign so far. And when it’s over, we have to keep ramping up for the final few months of the general election.

Yup’ik people also believe that when we set our mind to something, we can do anything. We use the word "ikayuquluta" when we work together to overcome challenges.

I firmly believe that, and I think we're at a point, certainly in Alaska, where we need to rise up and say we demand a Congress that helps all of us – not one that’s in it for their millionaire and billionaire donors.

That means we all have to do our part.

This team has been the backbone of this campaign since we launched just seven months ago, and I’m hopeful that this Primary Day will be no different.

So I have to ask again:

**[Can you make a contribution of $15, $25, $50 or whatever you can afford, during today’s primary election in Alaska to my campaign and Equal Opportunity Now? I have written a special, short note just for you to express my gratitude and outline our next steps.

### August 18, 2026 Newsletter
---
| | Back to School Special with Secretary of Education
---
| [](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=E064-lBgXz7jK3WyiYvaReFAMY50Q6RiflSm0UVTzeM.)
---
| | Moms are asking important questions about the future of education, the vital role of parents, and how we can ensure every child has a strong academic foundation.Who better to have this conversation with than U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon? Join us in Washington, D.C., for this special Back-to-School conversation as we discuss the progress being made to reshape education, the challenges facing our schools, and the vital role parents play in their children’s education. Secretary McMahon also shares her advice for families and her vision for the future of American education. Watch or listen to this important conversation with Secretary McMahon today! Full episode available now on [YouTube](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=oAyseRkb3LbQtyhTSoV5ivVrGD0BSiYHvXuV6bv--gA.), [Rumble](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=XRmueH1RgwqREH-z_KbD-h1780xznEIp-rHpMacZ3-Q.), [Spotify](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=607VpWdNPvvMokrmwC-Mo4iaAKrmiXKsriMsZ084eCI.) and [Apple](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=gjsl6FyZ2kRvb-W0sZ4_ZgIN5o9Ezxw1053r4KLd_r8.).
---
| | | |
---
| | How Moms Like You Can Energize and Influence Local Schools
---
| [](https://momsforamerica.us/so/f8Q0LElX_/c?w=6eemDbdeN5zJt_FVc1pFau6dwhUyHqrvTNbI2FFVC3Q.eyJ1IjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubW9tc2ZvcmFtZXJpY2EudXMvYmxvZyIsInIiOiJiMDI0MDM1OS1mNjk4LTRmZjctYTg1MS1iYWZiZTQ1ZTc1ZTEiLCJtIjoibWFpbCIsImMiOiJiMzgzOGJmOC1mYWIwLTQxYjktOTY3My1lOGM2YmVmYjY1NzcifQ)
---
| | As moms, worry comes naturally—especially when it comes to our children. When we see troubling things happening in our schools and communities, our protective instincts kick in. But what if God-given concern could become something more? Instead of worrying, what if you could take action? Moms for America is equipping moms to become School District Ambassadors—trusted, informed voices who help parents understand what’s happening in their local schools and give them the tools to engage wisely and constructively. You don’t have to be a political operative, a professional activist, or have hours of extra time. | | Dear Peter,

Greetings, my friend, and welcome to another installment of Transparency Tuesday!

Recently, I shared with you the news that I had officially filed a bill-draft request with the Nevada Legislature, bringing back my bill from last session that would create an Office of Inspector General, empowered to audit any entity that receives state funds. After all, you deserve to know your hard-earned tax dollars aren’t being wasted!

Well, I’ve got some more big news to share with you from the transparency front: I’ve also filed a request for a bill that would make labor negotiations in Nevada subject to the state’s Open Meeting Law.

Why is this important? Let me provide a little context...

As you may know, Nevada has an Open Meeting Law requiring deliberations of government bodies to be open to the public. As you might expect from a passionate proponent of government transparency, I think this is a very good thing.

However, what you might not know is that labor negotiations are currently exempted from the Open Meeting Law — meaning that the collective-bargaining process is conducted out of public view.

The bill I’ve requested would change that.

It should be obvious why this Open Meeting Law exemption is a problem. Personnel costs — public salaries and benefits (pensions included) — account for huge amounts of government spending. These costs are borne by you, the taxpayer. Yet because the negotiations over those costs aren’t covered by the Open Meeting Law, the taxpayers who foot the bill are kept in the dark as major decisions over how to spend their money are made.

I think that’s wrong, and unjust — which is why I’ve introduced this important bill to make collective bargaining open to the public. It’s your money they’re negotiating over, and you should have the right to observe that process!

By the way, I’ll take this opportunity to remind you that I’m up for re-election as Controller this year, and if I’m going to be around next legislative session to forcefully advocate for my transparency bills, I need to win this November.

You can help me achieve that goal by making a contribution to my campaign, [which you can do by clicking here](https://us.list-manage.com/FzaKi4vN2Mt?e=6736d7bc47&c2id=6d83a76682c29c59feb3e3d11de85f73).

Thanks for reading, my friend. I’ll be back in touch with you soon!

For Nevada’s future,

Andy

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18] | | | | | | The image you’re seeing in the news today isn’t what you think it is. **By Wendy M. Yurgo**
For decades, there was one subject American parents were effectively forbidden to question: the childhood vaccine schedule.
You could question what was in your child's food. You could question a prescription. You could demand a second opinion before surgery. You could refuse virtually any other medical intervention offered to your child. But question whether every vaccine, every dose, every combination, and every recommendation on the federal childhood schedule was necessary for your individual child, and suddenly the questions themselves became dangerous.
On August 10, President Donald Trump broke that taboo.
President Trump ordered the most significant reconsideration of federal childhood vaccine policy in decades, narrowing the vaccines recommended universally for all children and moving others toward risk based or shared clinical decision making. His administration framed the changes around parental choice, informed consent, and restoring trust in a public health system that lost enormous credibility during COVID.
The reaction was immediate and predictable. Pediatric organizations and public health officials warned that the changes could reduce vaccination rates and expose children to preventable diseases. Critics accused the administration of abandoning established science.
But underneath all of that outrage is a question that should have been asked a long time ago: When did questioning a government medical recommendation become forbidden?

My concerns about the childhood vaccine system did not begin with COVID, President Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., or Anthony Fauci. I began studying these issues in college and have continued studying them for decades. I watched the childhood schedule expand. I watched Congress construct a separate compensation system for vaccine injuries. I watched parents learn that some questions came with consequences. Eventually, I experienced those consequences myself.
When my family moved to Florida, finding a pediatric practice willing to care for my children became extraordinarily difficult because I did not follow the full CDC recommended vaccination schedule. The issue was not whether my children needed medical care. The issue was whether I would agree to someone else's vaccination schedule. Practices could simply decline to accept them as patients.
I am not a physician, and I do not pretend to be one. I am a lawyer and a mother. Perhaps that is precisely why the questions that have troubled me for decades are not only medical. They are questions about informed consent, liability, government power, institutional conflicts, transparency, and what happens when institutions entrusted with protecting children become hostile to the parents asking them to explain themselves.
My experience was hardly unique. The American Academy of Pediatrics has reported that 51 percent of pediatricians surveyed said their offices had policies allowing dismissal of families who refused vaccines in the primary series. Twenty eight percent reported policies permitting dismissal even when parents wanted to spread vaccines out.
Think about that. Parents were told vaccination was based upon informed consent while many families were simultaneously confronted with a very different message: follow the schedule or find another doctor.
That is not informed consent. And it is certainly not how trust is earned.
There is another question parents were rarely encouraged to ask: what did the testing actually look like before these vaccines became part of the childhood schedule?
Vaccines are tested before approval. That is not the issue. The issue is what parents reasonably assume the word "tested" means. Most parents would assume that a vaccine given to millions of healthy babies and children was tested against an inert placebo, in large numbers of children, with follow up sufficient to identify serious harm. That is not necessarily how vaccine trials are designed. FDA acknowledges that control groups may receive another approved vaccine, a placebo, or another substance. Prelicensure trials involving thousands of participants cannot possibly detect every rare adverse event that may emerge only after a product is administered to millions. That is precisely why postmarket surveillance exists.

So ask the questions. What did the control group receive? How many children were actually studied? How old were they? How long were they followed? What adverse events were captured? What was excluded? What remained unknown when the vaccine was added to the schedule?
These are basic questions. Yet parents asking them were routinely treated as though asking itself revealed ignorance.
Then came 1986.
President Ronald Reagan signed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act, creating an entirely different legal framework for injuries involving covered vaccines. Congress acted amid mounting litigation and concerns that manufacturers would leave the vaccine market. Instead of proceeding immediately through the ordinary tort system, families alleging covered vaccine injuries were directed first into a specialized federal compensation program.
As a lawyer, this has always troubled me. Liability is not merely about writing a check after someone gets hurt. The civil justice system creates accountability. Discovery opens files. Documents get produced. Witnesses sit for depositions. Lawyers ask what a company knew, when it knew it, what it tested, what it failed to test, and what it told the public. The threat of liability itself creates a powerful financial incentive to identify problems before consumers do.
Vaccines were given a different system.
Consider the structure. Government recommends the product. Government regulates the product. Government purchases enormous quantities of the product. States can condition school attendance on receiving the product. Pediatric practices may refuse to treat families who decline the recommended schedule. And when a covered vaccine allegedly causes an injury, Congress has created a specialized federal process that families generally must enter before pursuing ordinary civil litigation.
If virtually any other industry operated inside that structure, lawyers would immediately start asking questions about incentives, conflicts, transparency, and accountability.
Parents asked those questions about vaccines and were called anti science.
That is precisely backwards.
The greater the protection afforded a product and its manufacturers, the greater the obligation for transparency should become. The more government participates in recommending and promoting a medical intervention, the more rigorous independent scrutiny should become. And the more difficult ordinary accountability becomes, the more, not less, the public deserves to know about the evidence behind every recommendation.
Then there are the numbers no serious country should be afraid to examine.
At the beginning of the CDC's autism surveillance series, approximately one in 150 eight year old children in participating communities was identified with autism. By 2022, that number was one in 31.
One in 31.
There are legitimate scientific debates about how much of that staggering increase reflects expanded diagnostic criteria, earlier recognition, improved screening, genetics, environmental exposures, or other causes. Those questions deserve relentless scientific examination. But one in 31 is not a statistic that should be explained away with a slogan.
Parents have every right to ask what changed. What changed in children's environments? Their diets? Their chemical exposures? Their medicines? Prenatal exposures? Medical interventions? The childhood vaccination schedule?
Asking those questions does not establish the answer. It is how science is supposed to find one.

For too long, difficult questions surrounding vaccination were met not with more transparency, but more authority. Parents questioning the schedule were dismissed as anti-vaccine. Physicians and researchers challenging prevailing assumptions could find themselves marginalized. Public debate increasingly became a contest between institutional authority and those willing to question it.
The questions were not merely discouraged. They became forbidden.
Then COVID arrived.
Anthony Fauci became the embodiment of a public health culture that had grown increasingly comfortable demanding trust while treating skepticism as something to be managed. Guidance changed. Certainty remained. Legitimate scientific disagreements became political battles. Questions about laboratory origins, natural immunity, mandates, school closures, and other pandemic policies were too often treated not as questions worthy of examination but as threats to public compliance.
Then the records began emerging: emails, documents, private discussions, and Fauci's own pandemic diary.
On July 29, Fauci appeared under subpoena before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. More than a hundred times, the man who had spent years asking Americans to trust his judgment invoked the Fifth Amendment rather than answer questions under oath.
Fauci's lawyers maintain that the Fifth Amendment remains available despite his earlier pardon because new testimony could create new legal exposure. That may explain the legal strategy. It does nothing to change the spectacle: the man who spent years demanding the public's trust would not answer the public's questions under oath.
That hearing concerned COVID, but its implications reach far beyond it.
Public health depends upon public trust, and COVID exposed what happens when institutions mistake authority for credibility. Trust cannot be ordered from a podium. It cannot be enforced through access to a pediatrician. It cannot be manufactured by labeling parents ignorant, dangerous, or anti science because they want answers before consenting to a medical intervention involving their child.
Parents are not obstacles to their children's medical care. They are their children's advocates. And informed consent means very little if asking questions carries punishment.
That is why President Trump's action matters beyond the individual vaccines affected by it. For the first time in decades, the federal government itself is openly reconsidering assumptions surrounding the childhood schedule that parents were repeatedly told were beyond legitimate debate.
Critics may ultimately prove correct about some of these changes. Supporters may prove correct about others. Evidence, open scientific inquiry, and time should determine that.
What should never return is the idea that the questions themselves are forbidden.

You could question what was in your child's food. You could question a prescription. You could demand a second opinion before surgery. You could refuse virtually any other medical intervention offered to your child. But question whether every vaccine, every dose, every combination, and every recommendation on the federal childhood schedule was necessary for your individual child, and suddenly the questions themselves became dangerous. On August 10, President Donald Trump broke that taboo. President Trump ordered the most significant reconsideration of federal childhood vaccine policy in decades, narrowing the vaccines recommended universally for all children and moving others toward risk based or shared clinical decision making. His administration framed the changes around parental choice, informed consent, and restoring trust in a public health system that lost enormous credibility during COVID. The reaction was immediate and predictable. Pediatric organizations and public health officials warned that the changes could reduce vaccination rates and expose children to preventable diseases. Critics accused the administration of abandoning established science. But underneath all of that outrage is a question that should have been asked a long time ago: When did questioning a government medical recommendation become forbidden? Try it for yourself with a 45-day, no-risk trial. (Piece continues) My concerns about the childhood vaccine system did not begin with COVID, President Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., or Anthony Fauci. I began studying these issues in college and have continued studying them for decades. I watched the childhood schedule expand. I watched Congress construct a separate compensation system for vaccine injuries. I watched parents learn that some questions came with consequences. Eventually, I experienced those consequences myself. When my family moved to Florida, finding a pediatric practice willing to care for my children became extraordinarily difficult because I did not follow the full CDC recommended vaccination schedule. The issue was not whether my children needed medical care. The issue was whether I would agree to someone else's vaccination schedule. Practices could simply decline to accept them as patients. I am not a physician, and I do not pretend to be one. I am a lawyer and a mother. Perhaps that is precisely why the questions that have troubled me for decades are not only medical. They are questions about informed consent, liability, government power, institutional conflicts, transparency, and what happens when institutions entrusted with protecting children become hostile to the parents asking them to explain themselves. My experience was hardly unique. The American Academy of Pediatrics has reported that 51 percent of pediatricians surveyed said their offices had policies allowing dismissal of families who refused vaccines in the primary series. Twenty eight percent reported policies permitting dismissal even when parents wanted to spread vaccines out. Think about that. Parents were told vaccination was based upon informed consent while many families were simultaneously confronted with a very different message: follow the schedule or find another doctor. That is not informed consent. And it is certainly not how trust is earned. There is another question parents were rarely encouraged to ask: what did the testing actually look like before these vaccines became part of the childhood schedule? Vaccines are tested before approval. That is not the issue. The issue is what parents reasonably assume the word "tested" means. Most parents would assume that a vaccine given to millions of healthy babies and children was tested against an inert placebo, in large numbers of children, with follow up sufficient to identify serious harm. That is not necessarily how vaccine trials are designed. FDA acknowledges that control groups may receive another approved vaccine, a placebo, or another substance. Prelicensure trials involving thousands of participants cannot possibly detect every rare adverse event that may emerge only after a product is administered to millions. That is precisely why postmarket surveillance exists. PolitiBrawl is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a paid subscriber. So ask the questions. What did the control group receive? How many children were actually studied? How old were they? How long were they followed? What adverse events were captured? What was excluded? What remained unknown when the vaccine was added to the schedule? These are basic questions. Yet parents asking them were routinely treated as though asking itself revealed ignorance. Then came 1986. President Ronald Reagan signed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act, creating an entirely different legal framework for injuries involving covered vaccines. Congress acted amid mounting litigation and concerns that manufacturers would leave the vaccine market. Instead of proceeding immediately through the ordinary tort system, families alleging covered vaccine injuries were directed first into a specialized federal compensation program. As a lawyer, this has always troubled me. Liability is not merely about writing a check after someone gets hurt. The civil justice system creates accountability. Discovery opens files. Documents get produced. Witnesses sit for depositions. Lawyers ask what a company knew, when it knew it, what it tested, what it failed to test, and what it told the public. The threat of liability itself creates a powerful financial incentive to identify problems before consumers do. Vaccines were given a different system. Consider the structure. Government recommends the product. Government regulates the product. Government purchases enormous quantities of the product. States can condition school attendance on receiving the product. Pediatric practices may refuse to treat families who decline the recommended schedule. And when a covered vaccine allegedly causes an injury, Congress has created a specialized federal process that families generally must enter before pursuing ordinary civil litigation. If virtually any other industry operated inside that structure, lawyers would immediately start asking questions about incentives, conflicts, transparency, and accountability. Parents asked those questions about vaccines and were called anti science. That is precisely backwards. The greater the protection afforded a product and its manufacturers, the greater the obligation for transparency should become. The more government participates in recommending and promoting a medical intervention, the more rigorous independent scrutiny should become. And the more difficult ordinary accountability becomes, the more, not less, the public deserves to know about the evidence behind every recommendation. Then there are the numbers no serious country should be afraid to examine. At the beginning of the CDC's autism surveillance series, approximately one in 150 eight year old children in participating communities was identified with autism. By 2022, that number was one in 31. One in 31. There are legitimate scientific debates about how much of that staggering increase reflects expanded diagnostic criteria, earlier recognition, improved screening, genetics, environmental exposures, or other causes. Those questions deserve relentless scientific examination. But one in 31 is not a statistic that should be explained away with a slogan. Parents have every right to ask what changed. What changed in children's environments? Their diets? Their chemical exposures? Their medicines? Prenatal exposures? Medical interventions? The childhood vaccination schedule? clean_body: A week has passed since Wisconsin’s primary, and now that the results are in, one thing is clear: this election year is going to be unpredictable. | | | | | | | | A week has passed since Wisconsin’s primary, and now that the results are in, one thing is clear: this election is going to be unpredictable. Very few people expected Francesca Hong to fall short against David Crowley. The polling told one story. Election Day told another. That should be a wake-up call for every one of us. We have plenty of reasons to be optimistic about this November. Our fundraising pace is even stronger than 2022 > Josh Kaul has been barely visible on the campaign trail > Voters across Wisconsin are ready to make public safety top priority The opportunity is in front of us. Now we have to seize it. We just need to stay disciplined, focused, and aggressive from now through Election Day, November 3rd. Here is the plan to win: First, we have to keep meeting our monthly fundraising goals. Every deadline matters because every dollar helps us communicate with voters, respond quickly, and prepare for the fight ahead. Second, we need to draw a clear contrast between my record as a prosecutor and Josh Kaul’s record of failure. Wisconsin deserves an Attorney General who takes the job seriously, enforces the law, and puts victims, families, and communities first. Third, we must put public safety ahead of politics. Josh Kaul has spent too much time chasing political issues that do nothing to make Wisconsin safer. Voters need to hear that contrast clearly. And fourth, we need to produce strong, compelling ads that show Wisconsin is ready for change, while building the team needed to carry that message into every corner of the state. We win by doing the work now. The Wisconsin primary reminded us that anything can happen when voters start casting ballots. That lesson should make us sharper, more focused, and more determined than ever. So I am asking you directly: Wisconsin is ready for change. Now we have to prove we have the strength, resources, and grassroots support to make that change happen. Thank you, Eric Toney | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|---

I have good news and bad news. I am going to start with the good, because I think you deserve to hear it. **July was the strongest grassroots fundraising month of this entire campaign.** While Sabato's Crystal Ball was moving 14 races toward Democrats. While James Talarico's billionaire backers were writing $10 million checks. While the national environment was shifting against Republicans at every turn, Texas conservatives showed up in a way that I will never forget. You gave more in July than in any month since this campaign began. Not because a single mega-donor wrote a massive check. Because thousands of grassroots conservatives across this state and this country decided that Texas was worth fighting for. That is the good news. And it is genuinely great news. **Now here is the bad news.** **Fox News just released a new poll showing James Talarico leading me 51% to 48%. This is Fox News. Not a Democratic pollster. Not a liberal outlet._Fox News_. And their poll shows Talarico over 50% for the first time in this race.** Here is what the numbers show. Talarico has 98% of Democrats. He has 68% of independents. And 24% of non-MAGA Republicans are supporting him. That last number is the one that concerns me most. Nearly one in four Republicans who did not back President Trump is currently planning to vote for a Democrat who believes God is nonbinary, calls the American flag a complicated symbol, and wants a welcome mat at the southern border. **_I am not going to sugarcoat this. These numbers are serious._** But here is what I know. The margin of error on the Fox News poll is plus or minus 3 points. This race is not over. Among undecided voters, more lean toward me than toward Talarico. And the grassroots momentum we built in July proves that when conservatives show up, we can compete. The question is whether we can keep that momentum going into August... James Talarico has raised $70 million. He has the national media telling the story he wants told. **What I have is you, and the strongest grassroots month this campaign has ever seen.** Let us make August even stronger. Friend,

In Cypress, a broken and outdated storm water pump station was one heavy rain away from flooding neighborhood streets.

So I got $1,090,000 to fix it.

That's what Congress actually working looks like – something most people don't think is possible anymore. It’s not flashy or headline-worthy, and that’s how real governing should be.

This year alone, I've brought back over **$11 million in federal funding** to CA-45, and it's not sitting in some abstract "infrastructure" bucket. A few examples:
* **In Cypress:** Fixing that broken stormwater pump station to protect homes and roads from flooding.

* **In Fullerton:** Expanding the Hope Center to give unhoused neighbors shelter, job training, and a path off the streets.

* **In La Palma:** Upgrading critical public safety infrastructure and emergency communications.

* **In Westminster:** Renovating our Senior Service Community Center so older adults have a safe, welcoming place to gather.

* **In Cerritos & Buena Park:** Repairing the Del Amo Bridge and upgrading our local public library.

These are your tax dollars. My job isn't to let that money disappear into D.C. – it's making sure it comes right back home to strengthen our neighborhoods.

At the same time, key international buyers are leaving the U.S. market in response to the tariffs. It's a recipe for disaster.

At the same time, key international buyers are leaving the U.S. market in response to the tariffs. It's a recipe for disaster. Through it all, Miller-Meeks has been silent. body:
Up to $450 a year, for renters too. | |

Peter,

In most of Europe you can buy a small solar panel, hang it off your balcony, plug it into an ordinary outlet, and watch your power bill drop. In California, that was effectively illegal - _until now_.

My plug in solar bill has passed the Senate 35-1 and it's now one floor vote from the Governor's desk.

Here's why it matters: **California has the second-highest electricity rates in America, behind only Hawaii**. PG&E's rates went up nearly 40% between 2022 and 2025.

Every solution we've offered families for the last 20 years - _rooftop solar, panel arrays_ \- assume _you own a roof_. Millions of Californians don't. Most San Franciscans don’t.

**The utilities and the manufacturers both came at this bill. We negotiated hard and it got even stronger: consumer protection and cheaper power, in the same legislation in the end. **

This is what I mean when I say the affordability fight is not a campaign slogan - it's exactly the fight I'm taking to Congress - where the current majority is gutting clean energy credits and raising your costs to do it.

In a couple of weeks I will leave the State Senate for good. I can only keep doing this work and fighting for real solutions if this campaign is standing in November. If you believe in the progress we’ve made in California and want to see it spread across the nation - [**will you make your first donation of just $3 now to support this campaign?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137449973/640836558/-1931912562?refcode=SW_EM_FR_SOLAR_260818_1_1&amount=3&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MDY5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJlMmMyNGU3ZC0xNTliLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDBkM2ExMWZhMzAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=oVjzMDqiWXmzJaOsLgdYIFx8OhKudUZ_8P42AlRkU_o=)

Thanks for everything -
Let’s do this.

Scott

clean_body: Up to $450 a year, for renters too. | | Peter, In most of Europe you can buy a small solar panel, hang it off your balcony, plug it into an ordinary outlet, and watch your power bill drop. In California, that was effectively illegal - until now. My plug in solar bill has passed the Senate 35-1 and it's now one floor vote from the Governor's desk. Here's why it matters: California has the second-highest electricity rates in America, behind only Hawaii. PG&E's rates went up nearly 40% between 2022 and 2025. Every solution we've offered families for the last 20 years - rooftop solar, panel arrays \- assume you own a roof. Millions of Californians don't. Most San Franciscans don’t. The utilities and the manufacturers both came at this bill. We negotiated hard and it got even stronger: consumer protection and cheaper power, in the same legislation in the end. This is what I mean when I say the affordability fight is not a campaign slogan - it's exactly the fight I'm taking to Congress - where the current majority is gutting clean energy credits and raising your costs to do it. In a couple of weeks I will leave the State Senate for good. I can only keep doing this work and fighting for real solutions if this campaign is standing in November. If you believe in the progress we’ve made in California and want to see it spread across the nation - = Thanks for everything - Let’s do this. | | | | | | | | | | |
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
| Hi, it’s Jon Ossoff.Jon Ossoff
And James Talarico here.James Talarico |
| We’re reaching out because the path to a Democratic Senate majority runs through Georgia and Texas.Jon Ossoff
That’s right. There’s almost no chance we flip the Senate without Jon winning re-election and our movement beating Ken Paxton in Texas.James Talarico |
| That’s why MAGA Super PACs and right-wing billionaires are targeting us.Jon Ossoff
We expect our races in Georgia and Texas to be the two most expensive races _in the country._ James Talarico |
| And the most competitive.Jon Ossoff
[****We need everyone who cares about the Senate majority to please consider splitting a contribution between our campaigns today.****](https://act.electjon.com/go/5243?c0=ossoff-talarico-split-em.xvLVLZ&refcode=em260818-1-subs&utm_campaign=em260818-1-subs&t=2&akid=2706%2E5691347%2EILmbHi) James Talarico |
| Our only chance against the super PACs’ dark money...Jon Ossoff
...and the corporate cash and billionaire mega-donors....James Talarico |
| ...is with folks like you having our backs. [****Please split a donation today.****](https://act.electjon.com/go/5243?c0=ossoff-talarico-split-em.xvLVLZ&refcode=em260818-1-subs&utm_campaign=em260818-1-subs&t=3&akid=2706%2E5691347%2EILmbHi) Jon Ossoff
Jon and I are both in this fight to end the corruption in our political system. James Talarico |
| And to end the daily abuses and outrages of Donald Trump’s rule. As citizens, the next few months are the test of our lifetimes.Jon Ossoff
We are taking on the most powerful people in our country. People willing to spend billions to divide us.James Talarico |
| And that is why they’ll spend so much dark money to stop us.Jon Ossoff
Washington doesn’t want people like us who challenge the broken status quo. James Talarico | | | That’s exactly why I need James fighting alongside me in the U.S. Senate.Jon Ossoff
And it’s why we need to re-elect Jon.James Talarico |
| But it creates a massive challenge, right James?Jon Ossoff
Right. Hundreds of millions are going to flood into Georgia and Texas to buy these Senate seats. We’re counting on a grassroots movement to fight back.James Talarico |
| That movement is how we defied every pundit in 2020 to flip Georgia — a victory that secured the Senate majority.Jon Ossoff
And we’re about to do the same thing in Texas.James Talarico |
| In November, we’re going to prove them wrong again.Jon Ossoff
By winning Georgia and Texas to flip the Senate.James Talarico |
| [****So if you’re outraged by what’s happening to our country and you’re ready to fight back, please split a contribution between our campaigns today.****](https://act.electjon.com/go/5243?c0=ossoff-talarico-split-em.xvLVLZ&refcode=em260818-1-subs&utm_campaign=em260818-1-subs&t=4&akid=2706%2E5691347%2EILmbHi) Jon Ossoff
If everyone reading this chipped in even just a few bucks, we would have the resources we need to win our races.James Talarico |
| But not everyone does. So we’re counting on those who understand the stakes this November to step up.Jon Ossoff
Together, we can change this country.James Talarico |
**[CONTRIBUTE](https://act.electjon.com/go/5243?c0=ossoff-talarico-split-em.xvLVLZ&refcode=em260818-1-subs&utm_campaign=em260818-1-subs&t=5&akid=2706%2E5691347%2EILmbHi)**
* * *
Thank you in advance for answering our call. It means a lot.
— Jon & James —

disclaimer_text: Paid for by Vivek Ramaswamy and Rob McColley for Ohio
body:
If it came from Bernie, AOC, or Mamdani, don’t just question it - reject it outright. It’s a calculated lie.

| [](https://trk.email.vivekforohio.-sg)
---
Let me tell you something up front:
[I’m not a career politician. I don’t have all the answers – no one does. ](https://trk.email.vivekforohio.-gkJJeC3pzZ1DLu4fH3VQ)
What I DO HAVE, though, is the knowledge and understanding to determine the good ideas from the bad, what doesn’t work and why. Too many young people nowadays think “capitalism” is a dirty word.
They’ve been told that it’s a system that only benefits the rich and powerful – that socialism is the way of the future. It’s what Bernie Sanders, AOC, and Zohran Mamdani preach to their loyal followers.
But I’ll say one thing: If that’s coming from them, don’t just question it, reject it outright. It’s a calculated lie.
TRUTH IS: [Socialism has failed everywhere it’s been tried. It’s a system that stifles innovation, discourages hard work, and creates dependency on government handouts.](https://trk.email.vivekforohio.)
We need to do better than that.
I said this recently on Fox and Friends: Capitalism is the best system known to man. It lifts people out of poverty and rewards hard work, innovation, and entrepreneurship – and it's what made America the greatest country on earth.
That shouldn’t be a taboo thought or controversial opinion.
[It’s the exact reason that the American Dream even became possible! And the reason why I'm running to be Ohio’s next Governor.](https://trk.email.vivekforohio.)
I’m proposing a bold new agenda that will make Ohio the GOLD STANDARD for every state in the Union.
We're going to:

* CAP property taxes
* ELIMINATE income tax and capital gains tax
* CUT the red tape that's strangling our economy
* Ensure Ohio LEADS the next Industrial Revolution.

This isn't just about economics – it's about values. It's about embracing success instead of apologizing for it. It's about recognizing that the American Dream is within reach for EVERYONE, no matter where they come from or who they are.
But it’ll take a team to get it done.
[So I'm humbly asking for your help: Will you join me in the fight to make Ohio America’s gold standard?](https://trk.email.vivekforohio.-oxVMBjQ)

name: Barlow For Wyo
subject: Barlow For Wyoming Newsletter
body:
[Barlow Logo](https://barlowforwyo.com/)

Welcome to the Barlow for Wyoming Newsletter. Your hub for latest news, inf=
ormation and upcoming events.

=E2=80=8A

At the End of this Leg of the Journey...Gratitude

Hi friends,=E2=80=8BHere we are, folks.=C2=A0We made it to an important mil=
estone, the day of the Primary Election. And we didn't get here alone.=E2=
=80=8BOver the past year, Kelly and I have had the privilege of traveling t=
his great state, meeting thousands of Wyomingites, hearing your stories, sh=
aring your hopes, and talking about the future of the place we all love. We=
have been welcomed into your communities, your businesses, your ranches, y=
our farms, your coffee shops, your county fairs, your rodeos, and your home=
s. Every handshake, every conversation, and every mile has reminded us what=
makes Wyoming different.=E2=80=8BAround here, we still believe in looking =
people in the eye. We shake hands. We ask questions. We listen. If you want=
to understand Wyoming, you have to go where Wyoming is. That's exactly wha=
t Kelly and I set out to do, and it has been one of the greatest honors of =
our lives.=E2=80=8BOver the past two weeks, we've also been stopping at cou=
rthouses across the state to encourage people to vote. One statistic has st=
ayed with me throughout this campaign: for every person who voted in the la=
st primary, three friends, family members, or neighbors didn't.=E2=80=8BIf =
we want our government to represent the people well, then the people have t=
o represent themselves at the polls.=E2=80=8BThe primary election is August=
18. If you haven't already, make a plan to vote. Visit with your neighbors=
. Bring a friend. Encourage your family to participate. Our state is strong=
est when more Wyoming voices are heard.=E2=80=8BNo matter what happens tomo=
rrow, Kelly and I are deeply grateful. Thank you to every volunteer who gav=
e their time, every county chair who opened doors, every supporter who put =
up a sign, shared a post, made a phone call, or simply invited a neighbor t=
o a meet-and-greet. This campaign has been built by good people who care de=
eply about Wyoming, and we'll never forget that.=E2=80=8BWe're hopeful for =
what comes next. We hope to earn the opportunity to carry this conversation=
into the general election, but first comes the primary.=E2=80=8BThank you =
for trusting us with your time. Thank you for your kindness. Thank you for =
believing, as we do, that Wyoming's best days are still ahead.=E2=80=8BWe'l=
l see you at the polls.

Eric

In Case You Missed It...

Geringer Endorsement

Thank you to former Governor Jim Geringer for his support and kind words.

=E2=80=9CBut what has impressed me most about Eric =E2=80=94 and what I bel=

DOUGLASGreat day in Douglas for the Wyoming State Fair Parade and the Cente=
nnial Ag Celebration.We kicked off with a pre-party at the Willox home befo=
re the parade and finished with a celebration of 100 years of Wyoming agric=
ulture. There is no better reminder of what this state is built on.Thank yo=
u, Douglas, and congratulations to all those recognized today

GREEN RIVER

Sweetwater County welcomed us to their shrimp boil at the Green River Festi=
val, and what a kickoff it was!

Thank you to Lisa Herrera, Green River Chamber Director, for hosting a wond=
erful evening.

Kelly and I also had the chance to enjoy Art on the Green and even took hom=
e some fresh Wyoming artwork from local artists.

RIVERTON
Good meet-and-greet at Honey Fly Company in Riverton.

Great spot and great conversations with folks who came out to visit. Rivert=
on always brings good people to the table.

Thank you to everyone who came out.

RIVERTON

Young people from Boys & Girls Clubs across Wyoming came ready with good qu=
estions at the Governor Candidates Youth Town Hall in Riverton. We talked a=
bout jobs, mental health, community involvement, and how they can build mea=
ningful careers right here in Wyoming.

The best part was also getting to ask them a few questions. Listening to Wy=
oming=E2=80=99s young people matters. They know what they need and will tel=
l us.

Thank you to the Wyoming Alliance of Boys & Girls Clubs and the Boys & Girl=
s Club of Riverton for bringing us together.

Wyoming=E2=80=99s future was in that room.

=E2=80=8B

DOUGLASHonored to attend the Wyoming Ag Hall of Fame Awards Picnic and cele=
brate this year=E2=80=99s inductees, Mark Eisele and Ken Hamilton.Agricultu=
re is the backbone of Wyoming, and the men honored this week have dedicated=
their lives to strengthening and carrying on that legacy. Events like this=
remind us what this great state is built on.Congratulations to Mark, Ken, =
and all of this year=E2=80=99s honorees on this well-deserved recognition!

LARAMIE

=E2=80=8BA great evening at Mary and Rob Garland=E2=80=99s.

Kelly spoke about service in the everyday and what she would envision as Fi=
rst Lady. I had the chance to share what it means to me to serve in the Equ=
ality State.

Grateful for everyone who came out and for the warm hospitality.

LARAMIEWhat a visit to Wyo Tech.We spent time at their career fair with stu=
dents on the verge of graduating, sat in on classes, and learned about the =
programs the school offers. The trades and technical skills being built her=
e are exactly what Wyoming=E2=80=99s workforce needs. These students are ge=
tting to work and staying in Wyoming to do it.

RAWLINSWe stopped by the Carbon County Senior Center and visited with Execu=
tive Director Kelly Morrell. We also had the chance to visit with Copper Fr=
ance, a fourth-generation banker from Rawlins with deep roots in this commu=
nity and a long history with the bankers' association.=E2=80=8BWhile there,=
we had an encouraging visit at Memorial Hospital of Carbon County with COO=
Stephanie Hinkle and CEO Kerry Ashment.=E2=80=8BWe spoke about the challen=
ges they are tackling and the progress they have worked hard to achieve. Th=
e team at Memorial Hospital is doing the work to keep care close to home.=
=E2=80=8BThank you, Rawlins, for the warm welcome.

Along the campaign trail we toured several groups in Evanston, including Al=
ly Labs, APEX Designs, Evanston City Hall, and the great folks at the Senio=
r Center.=C2=A0=C2=A0

Ally Labs is a contract manufacturer producing personal care products for b=
rands across the country, right here in Wyoming. President Mike Gebs shared=
information on everything from formulation to packaging and scale-up.=C2=
=A0Mike said it best: =E2=80=9CI love the smallness of Wyoming, but that do=
esn=E2=80=99t mean you can=E2=80=99t do big things.=E2=80=9D That is exactl=
y the kind of Wyoming spirit we need more of.

APEX builds innovative aftermarket performance products for vehicle enthusi=
asts and ships them internationally, bringing money from outside directly i=
nto the Wyoming economy.=C2=A0When we asked what brought them to Wyoming to=
open their business, Paul Cox and Emmy said it all: =E2=80=9CFavorable tax=
base and polite young people."

Thank you to Senator Wendy Schuler and Jon Conrad for hosting a meet-and-gr=
eet at=C2=A0Purple Sage Golf Course in Evanston. This event brought togethe=
r candidates running for local office and folks who care about Wyoming=E2=
=80=99s future.=C2=A0

We made our way to Shell for a discussion on the politics of public lands.

Public lands are one of the most important issues facing Wyoming, and the f=
olks in Shell understand that better than most=E2=80=94good, honest convers=
ation about what is at stake and what leadership on this issue needs to loo=
k like.

=E2=80=8B

GILLETTE

Spent the morning in Gillette supporting the mobile food pantry.

School supplies and food are going out to families who need it most as the =
new school year approaches. Wyoming communities take care of their own, and=
it was good to be a small part of that

=E2=80=8B

CENTENNIAL

A good meet-and-greet on Saturday, led by volunteers at the Centennial Publ=
ic Library.

Folks came with concerns about access and emergency medications, exactly th=
e kind of rural healthcare gap that cannot be ignored. We also talked throu=
gh law enforcement and how communities handle issues like speeding on local=
roads.

BUFFALO

Over 130 people showed up for our meet-and-greet in Buffalo on Friday, and =
Kelly and I were blown away.

We covered a lot of ground: healthcare, leading with civility, and even som=
e lighter questions about the most memorable moments of this campaign.

That gave us a chance to reflect on some of the conversations we=E2=80=99ve=
had across Wyoming over the past year. You never know what someone=E2=80=
=99s most important issue will be until you ask. We=E2=80=99ve heard from a=
man concerned about keeping his pet snakes. We=E2=80=99ve heard from a hig=
h school senior in Casper who looked at us and said, =E2=80=9CI don=E2=80=
=99t think Wyoming wants me here.=E2=80=9D

That one has stayed with us.

Wyoming wants you here. Keeping Wyoming a place where our kids can see a fu=
ture for themselves is exactly why we are running.

Thank you, Buffalo

AFTON
Thank you to our volunteers who represented us at the Lincoln County Fair P=
arade in Afton.

This campaign is built on people who show up for Wyoming. We appreciate you=
so much!=C2=A0

CHEYENNE
We had the privilege of hearing from Sandra Bott and Andrea Allen from the =
Jae and Cowboy Cole Foundations.

We heard the stories of Jae and Cole, and both foundation=E2=80=99s mission=
to create what they call =E2=80=9CBoot-Check=E2=80=9D and =E2=80=9Cyellow =
feather=E2=80=9D moments across Wyoming, using cowboy boots and hat feather=
s to start conversations about mental health and suicide prevention.

The idea is simple and powerful. Slow down, check in on the people around y=
ou and how they=E2=80=99re feeling in their boots, and if they need a =E2=
=80=98pick up man=E2=80=99, a common rodeo term.

Kelly and I were honored to receive our own pair of Jae Boots. Mental healt=
h is one of the most important issues facing Wyoming families, and communit=
ies like ours need organizations doing this kind of work.

Learn more at [jaefoundation.com](http://jaefoundation.com)=C2=A0and [cowbo=
ycole.com](http://cowboycole.com)=C2=A0

ARCHER & PINE BLUFFS

Kelly and I stopped by the Laramie County Fair on our way to the Pine Bluff=
s Senior Center.

At the senior center, we discussed some of the negative ads circulating and=
why we have chosen to run this campaign the way we have.

The best days on this campaign are showing up and visiting with folks.

Thank you, Laramie County and Pine Bluffs

CHEYENNE
Great root beer float meet-and-greet at the Pointe in Cheyenne.

Good conversations with a big crowd of folks who came out to visit and hear=
where we stand. Grateful for everyone who took the time to be there.

CASPER

Thank you to Tim and Susan Stubson for hosting a meet-and-greet in Casper.

Great turnout with supporters and candidates from other races all in the sa=
me room. That is what this process is supposed to look like.

Grateful for the hospitality.

KAYCEE
There=E2=80=99s an old Johnson County bumper sticker that says, =E2=80=9CWe=
Haven=E2=80=99t Trusted Cheyenne Since 1892.=E2=80=9D History buffs of the=
Johnson County Cattle War know exactly what that means.

It's a healthy reminder that the best ideas don't usually come from the Cap=
itol.

In Kaycee, we tackled tough questions about education, Wyoming=E2=80=99s en=
ergy future, healthcare, data centers, and creating the opportunities that =
will keep our kids and grandkids here.

It was also good to reconnect with people I=E2=80=99ve known for years, inc=
luding many families I had the privilege of serving as their veterinarian.

Thank you to Lynn and Bob Harlan and Nancy Schiffer for hosting, and to eve=
ryone who joined us for an honest conversation about Wyoming=E2=80=99s futu=
re.

Celebration.We kicked off with a pre-party at the Willox home befo= re the parade and finished with a celebration of 100 years of Wyoming agric= ulture. There is no better reminder of what this state is built on.Thank yo= u, Douglas, and congratulations to all those recognized today GREEN RIVER Sweetwater County welcomed us to their shrimp boil at the Green River Festi= val, and what a kickoff it was! Thank you to Lisa Herrera, Green River Chamber Director, for hosting a wond= erful evening. Kelly and I also had the chance to enjoy Art on the Green and even took hom= e some fresh Wyoming artwork from local artists. RIVERTON Good meet-and-greet at Honey Fly Company in Riverton. Great spot and great conversations with folks who came out to visit. Rivert= on always brings good people to the table. Thank you to everyone who came out. RIVERTON Young people from Boys & Girls Clubs across Wyoming came ready with good qu= estions at the Governor Candidates Youth Town Hall in Riverton. We talked a= bout jobs, mental health, community involvement, and how they can build mea= ningful careers right here in Wyoming. The best part was also getting to ask them a few questions. Listening to Wy= oming=E2=80=99s young people matters. They know what they need and will tel= l us. Thank you to the Wyoming Alliance of Boys & Girls Clubs and the Boys & Girl= s Club of Riverton for bringing us together. Wyoming=E2=80=99s future was in that room. =E2=80=8B DOUGLASHonored to attend the Wyoming Ag Hall of Fame Awards Picnic and cele= brate this year=E2=80=99s inductees, Mark Eisele and Ken Hamilton.Agricultu= re is the backbone of Wyoming, and the men honored this week have dedicated= their lives to strengthening and carrying on that legacy. Events like this= remind us what this great state is built on.Congratulations to Mark, Ken, = and all of this year=E2=80=99s honorees on this well-deserved recognition! LARAMIE =E2=80=8BA great evening at Mary and Rob Garland=E2=80=99s. Kelly spoke about service in the everyday and what she would envision as Fi= rst Lady. I had the chance to share what it means to me to serve in the Equ= ality State. Grateful for everyone who came out and for the warm hospitality. LARAMIEWhat a visit to Wyo Tech.We spent time at their career fair with stu= dents on the verge of graduating, sat in on classes, and learned about the = programs the school offers. The trades and technical skills being built her= e are exactly what Wyoming=E2=80=99s workforce needs. These students are ge= tting to work and staying in Wyoming to do it. RAWLINSWe stopped by the Carbon County Senior Center and visited with Execu= tive Director Kelly Morrell. We also had the chance to visit with Copper Fr= ance, a fourth-generation banker from Rawlins with deep roots in this commu= nity and a long history with the bankers' association.=E2=80=8BWhile there,= we had an encouraging visit at Memorial Hospital of Carbon County with COO= Stephanie Hinkle and CEO Kerry Ashment.=E2=80=8BWe spoke about the challen= ges they are tackling and the progress they have worked hard to achieve. Th= e team at Memorial Hospital is doing the work to keep care close to home.= =E2=80=8BThank you, Rawlins, for the warm welcome. EVANSTON Along the campaign trail we toured several groups in Evanston, including Al= ly Labs, APEX Designs, Evanston City Hall, and the great folks at the Senio= r Center.=C2=A0=C2=A0 Ally Labs is a contract manufacturer producing personal care products for b= rands across the country, right here in Wyoming. President Mike Gebs shared= information on everything from formulation to packaging and scale-up.=C2= =A0Mike said it best: =E2=80=9CI love the smallness of Wyoming, but that do= esn=E2=80=99t mean you can=E2=80=99t do big things.=E2=80=9D That is exactl= y the kind of Wyoming spirit we need more of. APEX builds innovative aftermarket performance products for vehicle enthusi= asts and ships them internationally, bringing money from outside directly i= nto the Wyoming economy.=C2=A0When we asked what brought them to Wyoming to= open their business, Paul Cox and Emmy said it all: =E2=80=9CFavorable tax= base and polite young people." Thank you to Senator Wendy Schuler and Jon Conrad for hosting a meet-and-gr= eet at=C2=A0Purple Sage Golf Course in Evanston. This event brought togethe= r candidates running for local office and folks who care about Wyoming=E2= =80=99s future.=C2=A0 SHELL We made our way to Shell for a discussion on the politics of public lands. Public lands are one of the most important issues facing Wyoming, and the f= olks in Shell understand that better than most=E2=80=94good, honest convers= ation about what is at stake and what leadership on this issue needs to loo= k like. =E2=80=8B GILLETTE Spent the morning in Gillette supporting the mobile food pantry. School supplies and food are going out to families who need it most as the = new school year approaches. Wyoming communities take care of their own, and= it was good to be a small part of that =E2=80=8B CENTENNIAL A good meet-and-greet on Saturday, led by volunteers at the Centennial Publ= ic Library. Folks came with concerns about access and emergency medications, exactly th= e kind of rural healthcare gap that cannot be ignored. We also talked throu= gh law enforcement and how communities handle issues like speeding on local= roads. BUFFALO Over 130 people showed up for our meet-and-greet in Buffalo on Friday, and = Kelly and I were blown away. We covered a lot of ground: healthcare, leading with civility, and even som= e lighter questions about the most memorable moments of this campaign. That gave us a chance to reflect on some of the conversations we=E2=80=99ve= had across Wyoming over the past year. You never know what someone=E2=80= =99s most important issue will be until you ask. We=E2=80=99ve heard from a= man concerned about keeping his pet snakes. We=E2=80=99ve heard from a hig= h school senior in Casper who looked at us and said, =E2=80=9CI don=E2=80= =99t think Wyoming wants me here.=E2=80=9D That one has stayed with us. Wyoming wants you here. Keeping Wyoming a place where our kids can see a fu= ture for themselves is exactly why we are running. Thank you, Buffalo AFTON Thank you to our volunteers who represented us at the Lincoln County Fair P= arade in Afton. This campaign is built on people who show up for Wyoming. We appreciate you= so much!=C2=A0 CHEYENNE We had the privilege of hearing from Sandra Bott and Andrea Allen from the = Jae and Cowboy Cole Foundations. We heard the stories of Jae and Cole, and both foundation=E2=80=99s mission= to create what they call =E2=80=9CBoot-Check=E2=80=9D and =E2=80=9Cyellow = feather=E2=80=9D moments across Wyoming, using cowboy boots and hat feather= s to start conversations about mental health and suicide prevention. The idea is simple and powerful. Slow down, check in on the people around y= ou and how they=E2=80=99re feeling in their boots, and if they need a =E2= =80=98pick up man=E2=80=99, a common rodeo term. Kelly and I were honored to receive our own pair of Jae Boots. Mental healt= h is one of the most important issues facing Wyoming families, and communit= ies like ours need organizations doing this kind of work. Learn more at ARCHER & PINE BLUFFS Kelly and I stopped by the Laramie County Fair on our way to the Pine Bluff= s Senior Center. At the senior center, we discussed some of the negative ads circulating and= why we have chosen to run this campaign the way we have. The best days on this campaign are showing up and visiting with folks. Thank you, Laramie County and Pine Bluffs CHEYENNE Great root beer float meet-and-greet at the Pointe in Cheyenne. Good conversations with a big crowd of folks who came out to visit and hear= where we stand. Grateful for everyone who took the time to be there. CASPER Thank you to Tim and Susan Stubson for hosting a meet-and-greet in Casper. Great turnout with supporters and candidates from other races all in the sa= me room. That is what this process is supposed to look like. Grateful for the hospitality. KAYCEE There=E2=80=99s an old Johnson County bumper sticker that says, =E2=80=9CWe= Haven=E2=80=99t Trusted Cheyenne Since 1892.=E2=80=9D History buffs of the= Johnson County Cattle War know exactly what that means. It's a healthy reminder that the best ideas don't usually come from the Cap= itol. In Kaycee, we tackled tough questions about education, Wyoming=E2=80=99s en= ergy future, healthcare, data centers, and creating the opportunities that = will keep our kids and grandkids here. It was also good to reconnect with people I=E2=80=99ve known for years, inc= luding many families I had the privilege of serving as their veterinarian. Thank you to Lynn and Bob Harlan and Nancy Schiffer for hosting, and to eve= ryone who joined us for an honest conversation about Wyoming=E2=80=99s futu= re. Wyoming=E2=80=99s strength has always come from neighbors pitching in. Join= the Barlow For Wyoming team of volunteers who are helping share his messag= e across our state. =F0=9F=A4=A0 Ride with us =E2=80=94 sign up to volunteer! subject: BREAKING: My executive order to protect the Boundary Waters
